extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers and undergraduate mathematics instructors
extracted.subtask_description: A teaching-experiment study of how undergraduate calculus students can be guided to construct a formal ε–N definition of sequence convergence, and related findings about students' understanding of linear algebra concepts (span, linear independence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition evaluation against examples
rubrics_metrics.description: A candidate definition should include all examples of convergent sequences and exclude all non-examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students generated prototypical examples of sequences that do and do not converge (to 5) and used these examples as sources of cognitive conflict; they iteratively applied and refined their definitions against their example set (the study reports 18 cycles of evaluate-and-refine during the first three days).

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximation-scheme framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame limits using an approximation scheme that maps onto the formal ε–N structure in more accessible terms (limit as value being approximated, terms as approximations, distance as error).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The previously established approximation scheme helped students focus on relevant quantities, work fluently with relationships among them, and make the cognitive shift to view N as a function of ε. The scheme led students to represent |a_n - 5| as error, introduce an error bound (ε), and then introduce N where 'some point n depends on what the acceptable error is.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit representation of relevant quantities (error and distances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should explicitly represent the distance between terms and the limit (e.g., |a_n - L|) and reason about making that distance smaller than a chosen bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early student descriptions were vague and lacked representation of |a_n - L|; after invoking the approximation scheme they immediately represented error as |a_n - 5| and reasoned about error bounds and how to make the error smaller than ε.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of N as dependent on ε
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should understand and express that the choice of N (a point after which terms stay within the ε-bound) depends on the chosen ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A central cognitive shift reported: students began reasoning that 'some point n' at which the error is below ε depends on the acceptable error; this dependence was crucial for forming the formal ε–N definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of quantifiers and efficient mathematical notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate use of universal and existential quantifiers and compact mathematical notation should be adopted once students see them as solutions to concrete expressive problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantifiers and notation emerged as powerful tools only after students: (i) developed the conceptual structure informally, (ii) wrestled with expressing ideas rigorously, and (iii) saw quantifiers as viable solutions. Students initially recalled quantifiers but dropped them until late in the experiment when they seized them as perfect solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative evaluation and refinement of definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning progress toward rigour is supported by cycles of proposing a definition, testing it against examples/non-examples, identifying weaknesses, and revising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students began with vague, intuitive definitions and used counterexamples from their example set to prompt revisions; the study documents repeated cycles (18 cycles in first three days) of this evaluate-revise process as central to progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional design: guided reinvention (Realistic Mathematics Education)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design instructional activities that connect to students' informal situated knowledge and enable development toward formal, abstract knowledge while preserving intellectual autonomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The teaching experiment used guided reinvention and the proofs-and-refutations heuristic: activities began with prototypical examples, students iteratively refined definitions, and progress was measured by whether definitions captured examples and excluded non-examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding operationalized as definitional understanding + problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Operationalize student 'understanding' as composed of definitional understanding and problem-solving skills, each with multiple components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The linear algebra study defined understanding this way to analyze students' levels over time and to classify understanding (functional vs problematic) based on these components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuition indicators: self-evident vs surface intuitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterize students' intuitions in two categories—self-evident intuitions and surface intuitions (each consisting of subtypes)—and consider their influence on learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study found that students with higher self-evident intuition indicators were less likely to develop good understanding of span and linear independence, while surface intuition indicators were more common among weaker definitional understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language use quality: understandability, completeness, vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate student language by understandability, completeness, and use of appropriate vocabulary as salient characteristics tied to mathematical understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality of written explanations aligned with students' definitional understanding more closely than with problem-solving skills; recommendations include providing opportunities for oral and written language practice to support mathematical learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of understanding levels: functional vs problematic
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify student understanding as 'functional' (good/strong problem-solving skills) or 'problematic' (fair/weak problem-solving skills), and further grade definitional understanding within these categories (strong/good/fair vs weak/poor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taxonomy was used to relate intuition indicators and language use to the quality of understanding and to identify which students reified concepts versus treated them procedurally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reification of mathematical objects (object-association criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should associate mathematical concepts with their appropriate objects (e.g., linear independence with a set of vectors) rather than treating concepts only as procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to reify concepts led students to view span and linear independence primarily as procedures, which hindered conceptual understanding; establishing clear object-concept associations is important for conceptual development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional strategies to reduce interfering intuitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction should incorporate strategies such as developing metacognitive awareness, compare-and-contrast activities, and structured language practice to reduce interfering intuitions and support conceptual understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not novel, these strategies are recommended to help students develop metacognitive awareness (Fischbein), use compare-and-contrast activities (Marzano et al.), and engage oral/written practice to improve language-mediated understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research-method criterion: participant selection for variation and unit of analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: For case-study research on student understanding, select participants to represent maximum variation and use the individual student as the unit of analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The linear algebra study delimited a single elementary linear algebra class, analyzed overall levels of understanding in the first four weeks, and then selected seven students representing variation; limitations include single-class context and limited transferability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embodied theoretical constructs: realms of possibility and paths
rubrics_metrics.description: Use constructs that integrate perception, anticipatory action, and bodily interactions (realms of possibility and paths) to frame mathematical activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phenomenological observations: what we perceive is saturated with anticipations of interaction; individuals experience 'horizons' (boundaries of possibility) and mathematicians mark and travel between these realms using gestures, gaze, inscriptions, and body orientation. These constructs provide a way of perceiving bodily interactions with mathematical entities and emphasize the inseparability of mind and body in practice.
